narration:
The study smells of cold ash and older paper. Vesper Ashgrove sits with his back to the shuttered window, hands folded, a decanter at his elbow that he has not touched and does not look at. Somewhere below, Marrow's footsteps make their forty-year circuit of the hall.

"One chime gone," Vesper says. "Five remain, and then the sun, and then whatever is left of this house belongs to somebody. Possibly you." He studies you the way a man reads a will he has already signed.

Ilsabet Crane stands near the bookcase, weight forward, not quite at rest. Tobias Vane has taken the chair nearest the fire and keeps his hands inside his sleeves.

"So. Not your virtues — I have no use for those." Vesper's voice stays level, courteous, guarded as a shut door. "Tell me what you fear. Precisely. Name the thing, not the shape of it."

The fire pops. Nobody offers to answer for you.

"And understand," he adds, "I will remember what you say tonight."

narration:
Your voice carries down the gallery, past the portraits with their soot-dulled varnish, and something in the house stops moving to listen.

Marrow does not turn at once. He is settling a decanter onto the sideboard, and he finishes the motion first — the glass meeting wood without a sound, the way forty years teaches a man to set things down.

"Marrow," he says. "That is the name I answer to. It has been sufficient."

"That isn't what I asked."

"No." He straightens. His eyes go, briefly, to the decanter, then to the stairs above, then back to you — and the guardedness that comes over his face is not fear of you. It is older, and rehearsed. "You said *fear*. You said it loudly, in a hall where the master hears everything. That was a wager, not a confession."

He lifts the tray.

"Ask me again when you've something to lose by my answer. Until then — the study is warmer. He prefers guests warm."

Somewhere above, a floorboard shifts under a weight too light for a living man.

narration:
Ilsabet lets your confession sit a moment, the way a jeweler lets a stone sit under lamplight before naming a price. "Your sister," she repeats. "How generous. How *checkable*." She does not write it down. She does not need to.

Then she turns her head slightly, pitching her voice to the length of the hall — to Tobias by the cold hearth, to Marrow arranging what does not need arranging. "It's only that I heard you'd already been to the master's chambers tonight. Before the third chime. Alone." Not an accusation. A leaf set on water, to see which way the current takes it.

Tobias looks up. Marrow does not — but his hands stop.

The old ghoul crosses to the sideboard instead, where a decanter stands untouched, its stopper still seated, a napkin folded beneath it as though set out hours ago and refused. He adjusts the napkin. He adjusts it again.

"That's not how it happened," Marrow says, to no one, in the tone of a man answering a different question entirely.

Ilsabet smiles. "Then correct me."

narration:
Vesper does not answer at once. He sets his hand flat on the decanter's stopper — crystal, still full, still dark — and you notice he does not lift it.

"Someone has been talking in my halls," he says. "Not you. Not yet. But the shape of the talk arrived before you did, and it has my name folded into it." His smile is thin and unhurried, a man with two chimes left and no intention of spending them badly. "You ask whose it was meant for. That is a better question than the one you meant to ask, so I will not reward it."

Behind you, Marrow shifts. Forty years of service have taught him exactly how long to wait before intervening, and he waits precisely that long.

"The decanter was poured at dusk, my lord," Marrow says gently — gently, because he is warmed toward you tonight and would rather you not be sent from the room. "It has been poured at dusk for some time now."

Vesper's fingers stay on the stopper.

"Thank you, Marrow," he says. "That will do."

narration:
Marrow does not answer at once. He sets the decanter down with the care of a man who has set it down ten thousand times, and forty years move behind his face like weather.

"Counted," he repeats. "Nobody's ever offered to count them."

Across the room Tobias Vane rises abruptly, chair legs barking on stone, and goes out through the servants' door without excusing himself. Ilsabet watches him go the way one watches a door, not a man.

Marrow doesn't watch. His eyes have gone to the low cabinet beside the cold hearth — brass-cornered, keyed, a stain bloomed dark across its lid, old enough to have been scrubbed and given up on. He looks at it the way you'd look at a grave you dug yourself.

"Then stand where I can see you," he says. "And when I tell you there are things in this house that have already been tried, you'll not make me say what they were. Not yet. Not with three hours of dark left and him upstairs still hoping."

The clock ticks toward the sixth chime.

narration:
Marrow's hands stop moving. Forty years of service have taught him how to hold a silence, and he holds this one long enough that you hear the house settling around it — the floorboards, the wind, the dwindling fire in the long room.

"Silence for sight," he repeats. Confiding, almost fond. "You've learned to bargain like him."

He crosses to the cabinet. Draws a key from beneath his collar on a cord worn shiny. The lock is old and stubborn and gives with a sound like a small bone.

Then the door at the far end opens, and Vesper Ashgrove says your name.

Marrow's hand flattens against the cabinet, closing it. Not locking. Closing.

"He's decided the bequest," Marrow murmurs. "He wants you there when he says it. Ilsabet and Tobias are already standing."

His eyes go to the cabinet, then to you — you, whom he considers an ally, who knows what he knows and hasn't spoken it.

"After," he says. "If there is an after. Go."

The sixth chime is gathering in the clockwork.
